verse.text: Paul and Timothy, slaves of Christ Jesus, to all the holy ones in Christ Jesus who are in Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons:
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and “servant” softens it. In the Septuagint “slave of the Lord” is also a title of honour for figures such as Moses and David, so the word carries both lowliness and dignity. Many translations keep “servants”; others use “slaves” or “bondservants”.

“Saints” now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul uses the word of every member of the community, as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God's people” or “his holy people”.

The first term was an everyday word for a supervisor or official. It later developed into “bishop”, but here it is plural within a single city and refers to a group of local leaders. The second term, elsewhere simply “servant”, here names a recognised role in the assembly. The exact duties of either group at this date are not known.

verse.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
I thank my God every time I remember you,
always, in every prayer of mine for all of you, making my prayer with joy,
because of your partnership in the good news from the first day until now.
verse.note: “Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for the public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between “good news” and “gospel”.

verse.text: I am confident of this very thing: that the one who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.

It is right for me to think this way about all of you, because I hold you in my heart, for you are all partners with me in grace, both in my chains and in the defence and confirmation of the good news.

note.traditional: it is right / it is meet

verse.note: The adjective is the one this translation normally renders “righteous” or “just”. In the impersonal idiom used here it means simply “right” or “fitting”, and “righteous” would not be English. It belongs to the same word family as “righteousness” in verse 11; Greek has one family where English divides it between right/righteous and just/justice.

note.term: I hold you in my heart
note.traditional: I have you in my heart

verse.note: The Greek can equally be read “because you hold me in your heart”, since either pronoun can be the subject. The word order slightly favours “I hold you”, and most translations take it that way, but a few adopt the other reading.

verse.text: For God is my witness how I long for all of you with the deep affection of Christ Jesus.
And this is what I pray: that your love may overflow still more and more in knowledge and all insight,
so that you may discern what really matters, and so be sincere and blameless for the day of Christ,
filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.
Now I want you to know, brothers and sisters, that what has happened to me has actually turned out for the progress of the good news,
verse.note: The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as family, and this letter is plainly written to the whole community, women included (see 4:2–3). “Brothers” alone now sounds exclusively male. Several modern translations render it the same way; others keep “brothers”.

verse.text: so that it has become clear throughout the whole imperial guard and to everyone else that my chains are in Christ,
verse.note: The Greek borrows the Latin praetorium, which could mean a governor's official residence in a province or the emperor's praetorian guard in Rome. “Everyone else” suggests a body of people, which is why the guard is chosen here. Which is meant depends on where Paul was imprisoned. Rome is the traditional answer, but Ephesus and Caesarea have also been proposed, and the question is not settled.

verse.text: and most of the brothers and sisters, having gained confidence in the Lord from my chains, dare all the more to speak the word without fear.
verse.note: Many early manuscripts read “the word of God” and a few “the word of the Lord”. The SBLGNT prints the shorter reading, taking the longer forms to be scribal clarifications. The sense is the same either way.

verse.text: Some, it is true, proclaim Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill.
The latter act out of love, knowing that I am placed here for the defence of the good news;
the former announce Christ out of selfish ambition, not from pure motives, thinking to stir up distress for me in my chains.
What does it matter? Only that in every way, whether in pretence or in truth, Christ is announced, and in this I rejoice. Yes, and I will go on rejoicing,
for I know that this will turn out for my deliverance through your prayers and the support of the Spirit of Jesus Christ,
verse.note: This is the word rendered “salvation” in verse 28. Here it may mean release from prison, or Paul's final vindication before God whether he lives or dies; the next verse (“whether through life or through death”) leads many scholars to prefer the second. The clause echoes the Greek version of Job 13:16, where Job expects to be vindicated.

verse.text: in keeping with my eager expectation and hope that I will not be put to shame in anything, but that with all boldness, now as always, Christ will be honoured in my body, whether through life or through death.
For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain.
But if I am to live on in the flesh, that means fruitful work for me—and which I will choose I cannot say.
I am hard pressed between the two: I have the desire to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better;
but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake.
And confident of this, I know that I will remain, and remain with all of you, for your progress and joy in the faith,
so that your boasting in Christ Jesus may overflow on my account, through my presence with you again.
verse.note: The word covers both arriving and being present. It is the term used elsewhere for the coming of Christ and, in ordinary Greek, for the visit of a ruler. Here it refers simply to Paul's being with the Philippians again.

verse.text: Only live as citizens in a way worthy of the good news of Christ, so that, whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear about you that you are standing firm in one spirit, with one soul striving side by side for the faith of the good news,

note.traditional: let your manner of life be / conduct yourselves

verse.note: The verb means to live as a citizen and fulfil one's civic duties, though it could be used more loosely for conduct in general. Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens prized their status, and Paul returns to the image in 3:20. Most translations render it generally as “conduct yourselves”; a number of scholars and some versions bring out the civic sense, as here.

verse.text: and in no way frightened by those who oppose you. To them this is a sign of destruction, but of your salvation, and that from God;
for to you it has been granted, on behalf of Christ, not only to believe in him but also to suffer on his behalf,
as you face the same struggle you saw in me and now hear of in me.
So if there is any encouragement in Christ, any consolation from love, any sharing in the Spirit, any tenderness and compassion,
make my joy complete: be of the same mind, having the same love, united in soul, of one mind.
Do nothing out of selfish ambition or empty conceit, but in humility consider one another as above yourselves,
each of you looking not to your own interests but also to the interests of others.
Have this mind among yourselves, which was also in Christ Jesus,

note.term: which was also in Christ Jesus
note.traditional: which was also in Christ Jesus

verse.note: The Greek has no verb in this clause, so one must be supplied. The traditional reading, followed here, supplies 'was' and makes Christ's own attitude the model. Many scholars instead supply 'you have', giving 'think among yourselves the way you do in Christ Jesus', that is, as befits people who belong to him.

verse.text: who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to exploit,
verse.note: The word normally means the visible shape or appearance by which something is recognised. Whether Paul means divine nature, divine glory, or divine status here is disputed, and some translations paraphrase as 'in very nature God'. The same word returns in 'the form of a slave', so one English word is kept for both. Verses 6 to 11 are widely thought to be an early Christian hymn or poem that Paul quotes or composes.

note.traditional: robbery; a thing to be grasped

verse.note: Older versions have 'thought it not robbery', and many modern ones 'a thing to be grasped', which can suggest snatching at something not yet possessed. Studies of the Greek idiom 'to consider something a harpagmos' indicate it means treating something one already has as an advantage to be used for oneself. This is now the majority scholarly view, though the word is rare and the older readings still have defenders.

verse.text: but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, being born in the likeness of human beings. And being found in appearance as a human being,

note.traditional: made himself of no reputation; made himself nothing

verse.note: The Greek says simply that he 'emptied himself' and does not say of what. Most interpreters take the phrases that follow, taking a slave's form and being born human, as the explanation, so that the emptying is a self-lowering and not the surrender of some attribute. The literal rendering is kept because it echoes the 'empty conceit' of verse 3.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by another, and not for a hired servant. The contrast in the poem is between the highest status and the lowest. The related verb in verse 22 is rendered 'served as a slave' for the same reason.

verse.text: he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.
Therefore God also highly exalted him and granted him the name that is above every name,
so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth,
verse.note: Verses 10 and 11 echo Isaiah 45:23, where Israel's God declares that every knee will bow and every tongue swear allegiance to him. 'Lord' is the word the Greek Scriptures used in place of God's own name, so most interpreters take 'the name above every name' to be 'Lord'. The poem thus applies to Jesus language that Isaiah used of God alone.

verse.text: and every tongue acknowledge that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
So then, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not only as in my presence but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling,
for it is God who is at work in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure.
Do everything without grumbling or arguing,
so that you may become blameless and pure, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation, among whom you shine like stars in the world,
verse.note: The phrase comes from Deuteronomy 32:5 in the Greek version, where Moses describes Israel in the wilderness. The 'grumbling' of verse 14 recalls the same story. The word rendered 'stars' is the one used for the heavenly lights in the Greek of Genesis 1, and the image may also echo Daniel 12:3. Traditional versions have 'lights in the world'.

verse.text: holding fast the word of life, so that on the day of Christ I may boast that I did not run for nothing or labor for nothing.
verse.note: The verb can mean either to hold on to something or to hold it out to others. 'Holding fast the word of life' fits the context of perseverance. 'Holding out the word of life' fits the image of shining in the world. Translations and commentators are divided.

verse.text: But even if I am being poured out as a drink offering over the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice, and I rejoice with all of you.

note.term: poured out as a drink offering
note.traditional: offered; poured out as a drink offering

verse.note: In both Jewish and Greco-Roman worship, wine was poured out beside or over a sacrifice to complete it. Paul pictures the Philippians' faith as the main sacrifice and his own life, possibly his death, as the libation added to it.

verse.text: In the same way you too should rejoice, and rejoice with me.
I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may take heart when I learn how things are with you.
For I have no one like-minded who will genuinely care how things are with you,
for they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ.
But you know his proven character: as a child with a father he has served as a slave alongside me for the good news.
verse.note: 'Gospel' has become a purely religious term or a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, also used of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between 'good news' and 'gospel'.

verse.text: So I hope to send him at once, as soon as I see how things will go with me,
and I am confident in the Lord that I myself will also come soon.
But I consider it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother and coworker and fellow soldier, and your envoy and servant to my need,
verse.note: The Greek word is the one elsewhere translated 'apostle'. Here it has its ordinary sense of a delegate sent on behalf of others, since Epaphroditus was sent by the Philippian church with their gift for Paul. Most translations have 'messenger'. 'Envoy' is chosen because he was commissioned to represent them, not merely to carry word.

verse.text: since he has been longing for all of you and has been distressed because you heard that he was ill.
And indeed he was ill, close to death. But God had mercy on him, and not on him only but on me also, so that I would not have sorrow upon sorrow.
So I am sending him all the more eagerly, so that you may rejoice at seeing him again and I may have less sorrow.
verse.note: The Greek verb is in a past tense, as is 'consider' in verse 25. Ancient letter writers often wrote from the standpoint of the reader, for whom the sending would be past when the letter arrived. Epaphroditus was most likely the bearer of this letter, so English uses the present.

verse.text: So welcome him in the Lord with all joy, and hold such people in honor,
because for the work of Christ he came close to the point of death, risking his life to make up for what was lacking in your service to me.
Finally, my brothers and sisters, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is no trouble for me, and for you it is a safeguard.
verse.note: The Greek verb was also the ordinary word for both greeting and farewell, so the phrase could mean 'farewell in the Lord', and 'Finally' would then signal a closing. Because joy is a running theme of this letter, most translators take it as 'rejoice', as here.

verse.text: Watch out for the dogs, watch out for the evil workers, watch out for the mutilation.

note.traditional: the concision; those who mutilate the flesh

verse.note: Paul makes a bitter pun. The Greek word for circumcision is peritomē ('cutting around'), and he calls his opponents the katatomē ('cutting up'), a word related to the Septuagint's term for forbidden pagan gashing of the body. He then claims the title 'the circumcision' for those who worship by God's Spirit. The opponents are generally understood to be teachers urging circumcision on non-Jewish believers.

verse.text: For we are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God and boast in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh,
though I myself have grounds for confidence in the flesh as well. If anyone else thinks he can put confidence in the flesh, I can do so more:
circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew born of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee;
as to zeal, a persecutor of the assembly; as to the righteousness that is in the law, proved blameless.
verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of citizens and, in the Greek Old Testament, Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses 'assembly' throughout.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. The word covers being in the right, doing what is right, and in verse 9 a right standing that comes from God. Some scholars prefer 'justice' or 'covenant faithfulness' in English.

verse.text: But whatever things were gains to me, these I have come to consider loss because of Christ.

More than that, I consider everything to be loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. Because of him I have suffered the loss of everything, and I consider it dung, so that I may gain Christ
verse.note: The word was used in the period both for excrement and for refuse such as table scraps or scrapings thrown out. It was a coarse word in either sense. Most modern versions choose 'rubbish' or 'garbage'; the cruder sense is equally possible and fits the force of Paul's contrast.

verse.text: and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but the one that comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that rests on faith,
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'faith of Christ', and the grammar allows two readings: the believer's faith in Christ, or Christ's own faithfulness. 'Faith in Christ' is the traditional and still majority reading. 'The faithfulness of Christ' has substantial scholarly support, and on that reading the closing words 'that rests on faith' supply the believer's response.

verse.text: so that I may know him and the power of his resurrection and a sharing in his sufferings, being conformed to his death,
if somehow I may arrive at the resurrection from the dead.
Not that I have already obtained it or have already been made perfect, but I press on in the hope of taking hold of it, because I myself was taken hold of by Christ.

note.traditional: that for which (also I was taken hold of by Christ)

verse.note: The Greek connecting phrase can mean 'because' or 'that for which'. On the second reading Paul presses on to take hold of the very thing for which Christ took hold of him. Both readings are well supported, and the difference in overall sense is small.

verse.text: Brothers and sisters, I do not reckon that I myself have taken hold of it. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching out toward what lies ahead,
I press on toward the goal, for the prize of God's upward call in Christ Jesus.
So let all of us who are perfect be of this mind; and if on any point you are of a different mind, God will reveal this to you as well.
verse.note: The adjective means complete, full-grown or perfect, and most modern versions translate it 'mature' here. It is from the same root as the verb in verse 12, where Paul denies that he has 'already been made perfect', and the echo is kept here because it appears deliberate. Many scholars hear some irony: those who are truly 'perfect' know they have not yet arrived.

verse.text: Only let us keep in step with what we have already reached.
Join together in imitating me, brothers and sisters, and keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us.
For many walk, of whom I have often told you and now tell you even weeping, as enemies of the cross of Christ.
Their end is destruction, their god is the belly, and their glory is in their shame; their minds are on earthly things.
For our commonwealth is in the heavens, and from it we eagerly await a savior, the Lord Jesus Christ,
verse.note: In the usage of the period the word normally refers to a civic body, a state or a community of citizens, more than to the abstract status of citizenship. 'From it' refers back to this word in the Greek. Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens were enrolled as citizens of distant Rome, and 'savior' and 'lord' were titles given to the emperor. Many translations use 'citizenship', and some use 'commonwealth' or 'homeland'.
The Greek is plural, reflecting a Hebrew way of speaking about God's dwelling. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'. This translation keeps the plural wherever the Greek has it.

verse.text: who will transform our lowly body to be conformed to his glorious body, in keeping with the power at work that enables him even to subject all things to himself.
So then, my brothers and sisters, beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, beloved.
verse.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of siblings or fellow members. Paul goes on at once to name two women of the community, so 'brothers' alone would now suggest a narrower audience than his readers understood. Many recent translations make the same choice; others keep 'brothers' with a footnote.

verse.text: I urge Euodia and I urge Syntyche to be of one mind in the Lord.
Yes, and I ask you also, true partner, to help these women, who contended at my side in the good news, along with Clement and the rest of my co-workers, whose names are in the book of life.
verse.note: The word means someone yoked together with another, a close partner in work. Paul does not name the person, and the Philippians evidently knew who was meant. Some scholars take the word as a proper name, Syzygus, with a play on its meaning ('you who are a partner in fact as in name'), but the name is not attested elsewhere.

The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' has since become a purely religious term and a book title. Many modern translations already alternate between the two renderings.

verse.text: Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: rejoice!
Let your forbearance be known to all people. The Lord is near.
verse.note: The Greek can mean near in time (the Lord's coming is soon, as in 3:20) or near in presence (the Lord is close to those who call on him, as in Psalm 145:18). The sentence may be read with what precedes or what follows, and Paul may intend both senses. The rendering leaves the question open as the Greek does.

verse.text: Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will stand guard over your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

Finally, brothers and sisters, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovable, whatever is well spoken of, if there is any excellence and if there is anything worthy of praise, dwell on these things.
verse.note: Several terms in this list, and this one above all, belong to the common vocabulary of Greek moral teaching, not to the special vocabulary of the Septuagint. This is the only place Paul uses the word, the standard Greek term for moral excellence. He appears to be telling the Philippians to take account of whatever their wider culture rightly recognizes as good.

verse.text: What you learned and received and heard and saw in me, put these things into practice, and the God of peace will be with you.
I rejoiced greatly in the Lord that now at last your concern for me has blossomed again; you were indeed concerned, but you had no opportunity.
Not that I say this out of want, for I have learned to be self-sufficient in whatever circumstances I am in.
verse.note: The word was the standard term, prized especially by Stoic and Cynic teachers, for a person who is independent of circumstances and needs nothing from outside. Most translations use 'content', which is a recognized sense, but it loses the echo a first-century reader would have heard. Verse 13 then gives the twist: Paul's sufficiency comes not from himself but from the one who empowers him.

verse.text: I know how to be brought low, and I know how to have more than enough. In each and every circumstance I have been initiated into being well fed and going hungry, into having more than enough and being in want.

note.traditional: I have learned the secret / I am instructed

verse.note: The verb is the technical term for initiation into a mystery cult, used only here in the New Testament. Paul uses it figuratively: plenty and want alike are rites he has been through. Most translations paraphrase as 'learned the secret', which conveys the sense but hides the image.

verse.text: I have strength for all things in the one who empowers me.

note.term: I have strength for all things

verse.note: The verb means to be strong or to have power for something. 'All things' looks back to the circumstances just listed, hunger and plenty, want and abundance; the sentence is about enduring any situation, not accomplishing any goal. 'I can do all things' is a fair rendering and is the mainstream one, though it is often read out of context. Later manuscripts add 'Christ' after 'the one who empowers me', whence the familiar 'through Christ'; the earliest text leaves him unnamed.

verse.text: Even so, you did well to share in my affliction.
And you Philippians yourselves know that in the early days of the good news, when I left Macedonia, no assembly shared with me in an account of giving and receiving except you alone;
verse.note: A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering of citizens and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is near-universal in English and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses 'assembly' wherever the word occurs.

note.term: an account of giving and receiving
note.traditional: in the matter of giving and receiving

verse.note: Paul uses the language of business throughout this passage. 'Account of giving and receiving' was a bookkeeping expression for credits and debits; 'fruit that accrues to your account' in verse 17 is the language of profit or interest; and 'I have received in full' in verse 18 is the formula written on receipts. He describes the Philippians' gift as a partnership, with the return credited to them by God.

verse.text: for even in Thessalonica you sent something for my need, once and then again.
Not that I seek the gift; rather, I seek the fruit that accrues to your account.
I have received everything in full and have more than enough. I am filled, now that I have received from Epaphroditus what came from you, a fragrant aroma, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God.

note.traditional: an odour of a sweet smell / a fragrant offering

verse.note: This is the Septuagint's stock phrase for the smoke of a sacrifice rising pleasingly to God (for example Genesis 8:21 and often in Leviticus). Paul turns from commercial to temple language: the money sent to him is in truth an offering made to God.

verse.text: And my God will fill your every need according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.
To our God and Father be the glory to the ages of the ages. Amen.

note.term: to the ages of the ages

verse.note: The Greek is a Semitic-style superlative, literally 'into the ages of the ages', meaning through all ages without end. 'For ever and ever' gives the sense and is the usual rendering. The literal form is kept here because this translation preserves such turns of phrase where the Greek has them.

verse.text: Greet every holy one in Christ Jesus. The brothers and sisters who are with me greet you.
verse.note: Paul uses this word for every member of the community, as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saint' now suggests a canonized individual or a person of exceptional virtue. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

verse.text: All the holy ones greet you, especially those of Caesar's household.
verse.note: This was the usual term for the emperor's large staff of slaves and freed slaves who ran the imperial administration, in Rome and in the provinces. It does not mean members of the emperor's family. Philippi was a Roman colony, and a greeting from believers in imperial service would have carried particular weight there.

verse.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
